segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, look, magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star at its rising and have come to pay him homage.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When King Herod heard this, he was alarmed, and all Jerusalem with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Messiah was to be born.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They told him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written through the prophet:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the leaders of Judah; for out of you will come a leader who will shepherd my people Israel.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Herod secretly summoned the magi and carefully ascertained from them the time of the star’s appearing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he sent them to Bethlehem, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and pay him homage.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After hearing the king, they set out, and look, the star they had seen at its rising went ahead of them until it came and stood over the place where the child was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Entering the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and paid him homage. Then, opening their treasure chests, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they withdrew to their own country by another road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After they had withdrawn, look, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child to destroy him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he got up, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he was there until Herod’s death, so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Herod, seeing that he had been made a fool of by the magi, was furious, and he sent and killed all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its surrounding district who were two years old and under, according to the time he had carefully ascertained from the magi.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation: Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After Herod died, look, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child’s life have died.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he got up, took the child and his mother, and went into the land of Israel.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the region of Galilee,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he came and settled in a town called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.

notes.note: This is Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as a client king under Rome and died in 4 BC. He was known for great building projects, including the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple, and for ruthlessness toward anyone he saw as a rival, including members of his own family.

The Greek word originally named a Persian priestly class and by this period was used for eastern experts in astrology, dream interpretation and similar arts. “Wise men” is too general, and the text says nothing of their being kings or three in number. Several modern translations also use “Magi”. The same word can be used negatively of a sorcerer, as in Acts 13.

The Greek word means both “rising” (of a heavenly body) and “east”. In verse 1 “from the east” uses the plural without the article, the usual idiom for the direction. Here the singular with the article more naturally refers to the star’s rising, a technical astronomical expression. Most recent translations agree, though “in the east” remains possible.

The verb describes bowing or prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a king or a god. The magi are looking for a newborn king, and Herod uses the same word in verse 8, so royal homage is the sense on the characters’ lips. Many interpreters think Matthew intends his readers to see more in the act than the magi knew, and “worship” is the long-standing rendering.

Herod is asking about a title, the anointed king whom Israel expected, not using a name for Jesus. “Messiah” conveys that title to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” sounds like a proper name. Several modern translations make the same distinction, using “Messiah” where the title is under discussion and “Christ” elsewhere.

The quotation is from Micah 5:2, with a final line that echoes 2 Samuel 5:2 on David as shepherd of Israel. Its wording differs from both the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament, which describe Bethlehem as small among the clans of Judah. In Matthew’s form the town is no longer insignificant because of the ruler who comes from it.

notes.phrase: Out of Egypt I called my son
notes.note: The quotation is Hosea 11:1, where “my son” is the people of Israel brought out of Egypt in the exodus. Matthew presents Jesus as retracing Israel’s story. The wording follows the Hebrew text and not the Greek Old Testament, which reads “his children”.

The Greek noun is in the masculine plural, and since Herod is hunting a male rival, most modern translations render it “boys” or “male children”. The older English tradition has “children”. A masculine plural can in principle cover both sexes, but the context favours the narrower sense.

The quotation is Jeremiah 31:15, a lament over Israelites going into exile, with Ramah, a town north of Jerusalem, as its setting. Rachel, wife of Jacob, is pictured as the mother of the nation mourning her descendants. Genesis places her burial on the road to Bethlehem, which helps explain the link Matthew draws.

On Herod’s death his territory was divided among his sons. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea with the lesser title of ethnarch, so “reigning” is used loosely. His rule was harsh enough that Rome removed him in AD 6. Galilee fell to his brother Herod Antipas.

notes.phrase: that he would be called a Nazarene
notes.traditional: He shall be called a Nazarene
notes.note: No Old Testament passage contains these words, and Matthew refers to “the prophets” in the plural, so this is rendered as a summary and not a direct quotation. The Greek allows either. What Matthew has in mind is disputed: common proposals are a wordplay on the Hebrew for “branch” in Isaiah 11:1, or on “nazirite” as in Judges 13:5. The Greek form is sometimes spelled “Nazorean” in English.

candidates.reason: Positive in Matthew 2 but negative in Acts 13:6, 8 (“sorcerer”), so a decision is needed on whether to split the rendering and how to explain it.
The verb ranges from bowing to a superior to worship of God, and translators differ on where to put “worship”. Uncontrolled variation across the Gospels and Revelation would mislead.
“Scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers, where the Greek means a trained expert in the Law. It recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts and needs one rendering.
Extremely frequent as a narrative attention-marker. Translators vary between “behold”, “look”, “suddenly” and omission, and a single policy is needed.
It covers God (standing for the divine name in Old Testament quotations and phrases like “angel of the Lord”), Jesus, and ordinary “sir/master”. The boundaries between these need a consistent policy.
